children: Poland's manufacturing sector contracted for a 16th straight month in August, while Hungarian factory output also weakened, but the Czech manufacturing business sentiment jumped to a more than four-year high on strong output and orders.

The S&P Global Poland Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 48.3 in August from 49.0 in July, sliding further below the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction, as output and new orders fell faster and supply-chain pressures intensified amid the Iran war.

The Czech PMI rose to 54.1 in August from 52.2 in July, marking the strongest reading since April 2022, while Hungary's seasonally adjusted PMI edged down to 51.3 in August from 51.4 in July, although it still signalled expansion.

"The only positive to take from the latest (Polish) survey was a further improvement in the 12-month outlook for production, though expectations remained weak relative to the long-run trend," Trevor Balchin, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said.

Hungary's August figure fell short of a long-term monthly average of 52.7 but was higher than an average 49.7 August reading in the past three years, the Association of Logistics, Purchasing and Inventory Management said.

Final data for second-quarter GDP in Hungary, released on Tuesday by the Central Statistics Office, underpinned the positive outlook, ING analyst Peter Virovacz said, projecting a 1.7% economic growth this year.

"Consumption may be the engine of the Hungarian economy throughout the year, while investment may show a slight increase if the investment statistics at the end of the year are pushed by EU cash flow," he said.
"In 2027-2028, the further recovery of domestic demand and the final resumption of external demand may bring GDP growth of around 3.0%.

Romania's manufacturing PMI rose for a second consecutive month in August to 51.1 from 50.1 in July, data from Romania’s BCR bank showed, pointing to a gradual strengthening in manufacturing activity.
